nodes.title: CAPITAL STRATEGY
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses American Express's capital strategy, focusing on how the company allocates and manages capital to support business growth, maintain regulatory compliance, and generate shareholder value. Key points include:

- The objective to retain sufficient capital from net income and other sources to maintain a strong balance sheet, support future growth, and return excess capital to shareholders via dividends and share repurchases.
- The use of an Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process to determine capital levels, considering business activities, market conditions, and regulatory requirements.
- Adherence to U.S. federal banking regulations, including specific capital adequacy guidelines set by the Federal Reserve, and the importance of maintaining capital ratios above minimum regulatory requirements to preserve financial holding company status.
- Targeting a Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) risk-based capital ratio in the 10-11% range.
- Flexibility to shift capital among subsidiaries to meet targeted capital levels and regulatory requirements.
- Reporting of capital ratios under Basel III definitions and the standardized approach for risk-weighted assets.
- Presentation of detailed regulatory risk-based capital and leverage ratios for both American Express Company and its U.S. bank subsidiary as of December 31, 2022, showing that both exceed minimum requirements.
- Definitions and explanations of key regulatory capital ratios (CET1, Tier 1, Total Risk-Based Capital, and Tier 1 Leverage), including the impact of the Current Expected Credit Loss (CECL) methodology and the phase-in of its effects on regulatory capital.
- Participation in the Federal Reserve’s supervisory stress tests and confirmation of the company’s stress capital buffer (SCB), resulting in a minimum CET1 ratio of 7% effective October 1, 2022.

nodes.title: DIVIDENDS AND SHARE REPURCHASES
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the company's approach to returning capital to common shareholders through dividends and share repurchases. It details the amounts distributed in 2022, including $1.6 billion in dividends and $3.3 billion in share repurchases, totaling 64% of the capital generated that year. The company repurchased 20 million shares at an average price of $168.14 and plans to increase its quarterly dividend by 15% in 2023. It also notes $57 million in dividends paid on preferred shares. The document outlines factors influencing capital distribution decisions, such as regulatory requirements, business results, and market conditions, and describes various methods for conducting share repurchases.

nodes.title: FUNDING STRATEGY
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the company's funding strategy, emphasizing the importance of maintaining a broad and diversified range of funding sources to support global business operations and ensure strong liquidity. It explains that funding needs are primarily driven by the proprietary card-issuing business, which requires financing merchant payments before reimbursement from card members. The strategy integrates funding activities with asset-liability management and includes a comprehensive funding policy for the company and its subsidiaries. The document highlights the use of various funding instruments—such as deposits, unsecured debt, asset securitizations, and secured borrowing facilities—to achieve diversity, cost efficiency, and resilience against market disruptions. It also notes the expectation of continued growth in direct deposits and the importance of managing a balanced debt maturity profile to meet both short-term and long-term refinancing needs.

nodes.title: FUNDING PROGRAMS AND ACTIVITIES
nodes.summary: This partial document discusses the company's funding programs and activities, focusing on customer deposits and consolidated debt as of December 31 for the years 2022 and 2021. It provides a summary table showing the amounts of customer deposits, short-term borrowings, long-term debt, and total customer deposits and debt. The document outlines the company's funding plan for 2023, including targeted amounts for unsecured and secured term debt issuance. It also notes that actual funding activities may differ from plans due to factors such as business growth, economic and political events, market demand, regulatory changes, and loan performance. Additionally, the document highlights the importance of maintaining strong credit ratings from major agencies to support access to cost-effective funding and mentions that asset securitization activities are rated separately.

nodes.title: TABLE 19: UNSECURED DEBT RATINGS
nodes.summary: The partial document provides a table summarizing the unsecured debt ratings for various American Express entities, including American Express Company, American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc., American Express National Bank, and American Express Credit Corporation. The table lists long-term and short-term credit ratings, as well as outlooks, from Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch. The document notes that these ratings are not investment recommendations and may change at the discretion of the rating agencies. It also discusses the potential negative impacts of credit rating downgrades, such as increased funding costs and reduced borrowing capacity, but states that the company’s funding mix, particularly the proportion of FDIC-insured U.S. retail deposits, should help mitigate these effects.

nodes.title: DEPOSIT PROGRAMS
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the deposit programs offered by the company's U.S. bank subsidiary, AENB. It highlights that deposits are FDIC-insured up to at least $250,000 per account holder and that the ability to offer competitive rates depends on AENB's capital level. The primary deposit products are direct retail deposits, including high-yield savings accounts and certificates of deposit (CDs), with additional checking account products and deposits sourced through third-party channels as needed. As of December 31, 2022, total deposits amounted to $110.2 billion. The document also references further details in the consolidated financial statements.

nodes.title: SHORT-TERM FUNDING PROGRAMS
nodes.summary:
## SHORT-TERM FUNDING PROGRAMS

Short-term borrowings, such as commercial paper, are defined as any debt with an original maturity of twelve months or less, as well as interest-bearing overdrafts with banks. Our short-term funding programs are used primarily to fund working capital needs, such as managing seasonal variations in receivables balances. The amount of short-term borrowings issued in the future will depend on our funding strategy, our needs and market conditions. We had no commercial paper outstanding at any point during 2022. Refer to Note 8 to the "Consolidated Financial Statements" for a further description of these borrowings.

nodes.title: LONG-TERM DEBT AND ASSET SECURITIZATION PROGRAMS
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the company's long-term debt and asset securitization programs as of December 31, 2022. It reports a total of $42.6 billion in long-term debt, which includes both unsecured debt and asset-backed securities. The document explains the process and purpose of securitizing Card Member loans and receivables, highlighting that these are transferred to a trust that issues securities to third-party investors, providing the company with cost-effective funding. A table summarizes the company's 2022 debt issuances, detailing various types of notes and certificates issued by American Express Company and its Credit Account Master Trust, with a total issuance of $20.5 billion. The table includes information on coupon rates and references the secured overnight financing rate (SOFR) for floating rate instruments. The document also refers readers to specific notes in the consolidated financial statements for more detailed information.

nodes.title: LIQUIDITY MANAGEMENT
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the company's approach to liquidity management, emphasizing the objective of maintaining access to a diverse range of on- and off-balance sheet liquidity sources sufficient to meet financial obligations for at least twelve months during adverse economic conditions. Key elements of the strategy include diversifying funding sources, holding unencumbered liquid assets, projecting cash flows under various scenarios, and complying with regulatory requirements. The document outlines the use of stress testing, including scenarios mandated by the Dodd-Frank Act and internal policies, to determine appropriate liquidity levels. It also notes that the investment income from liquidity resources is typically less than the cost of funding them, with future net interest income dependent on the amount of liquidity maintained and the spread between funding costs and investment yields.

nodes.title: Securitized Borrowing Capacity
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the company's securitized borrowing capacity as of December 31, 2022. It details two committed, revolving, secured borrowing facilities: one allowing the sale of up to $3.0 billion in AAA notes from the American Express Issuance Trust II (maturing July 15, 2024), and another allowing the sale of up to $2.0 billion in AAA certificates from the American Express Credit Account Master Trust (maturing September 16, 2024). These facilities are used for working capital and to enhance contingent funding resources. As of the reporting date, no amounts had been drawn from either facility.

nodes.title: Federal Reserve Discount Window
nodes.summary:
## Federal Reserve Discount Window

As an insured depository institution, AENB may borrow from the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, subject to the amount of qualifying collateral that it may pledge. The Federal Reserve has indicated that both credit and charge card receivables are a form of qualifying collateral for secured borrowings made through the discount window. Whether specific assets will be considered qualifying collateral and the amount that may be borrowed against the collateral remain at the discretion of the Federal Reserve.

As of December 31, 2022, we had approximately $\$ 102.8$ billion in U.S. credit card loans and charge card receivables that could be sold over time through our securitization trusts or pledged in return for secured borrowings to provide further liquidity, subject in each case to applicable market conditions and eligibility criteria.

nodes.title: Committed Bank Credit Facility
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the company's committed syndicated bank credit facility of $3.5 billion as of December 31, 2022, with a maturity date of October 15, 2024. It outlines the conditions for accessing the facility, specifically the requirement to maintain a minimum CET1 risk-based capital ratio of 4.5%, and notes restrictions if the ratio falls between 4.5% and 6.5%. The facility does not include a material adverse change clause or depend on the company's credit rating. As of the reporting date, the company was in compliance with all covenants and had not drawn any amounts. The facility is used for working capital needs and can backstop outstanding commercial paper.

nodes.title: Off-balance Sheet Arrangements
nodes.summary:
## Off-balance Sheet Arrangements

We have certain off-balance sheet obligations that include guarantees, indemnifications and certain Card Member and partner arrangements that may have a material current or future effect on our financial condition, changes in financial condition, results of operations, or liquidity and capital resources. For more information on these obligations, refer to Note 12, Note 15 and Note 23 to the "Consolidated Financial Statements."

nodes.title: CASH FLOWS
nodes.summary: The partial document provides a summary of the company's cash flow activities for the years 2022, 2021, and 2020. It includes a table showing cash provided by or used in operating, investing, and financing activities, as well as the effect of foreign currency exchange rates on cash and cash equivalents. The document highlights significant changes in cash flows between the years, with notable increases in cash from operating and financing activities in 2022, a substantial outflow from investing activities, and the resulting net increase or decrease in cash and cash equivalents for each year. The section also indicates that a discussion follows regarding the major factors driving these cash flow changes between 2022 and 2021.

nodes.title: Cash Flows from Operating Activities
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the company's cash flows from operating activities, explaining that these are mainly influenced by net income adjusted for non-cash items (such as provisions for credit losses, depreciation, amortization, stock-based compensation, and deferred taxes) and changes in operating assets and liabilities. It highlights that in both 2022 and 2021, net cash provided by operating activities was primarily driven by cash generated from net income and increases in net operating liabilities, particularly due to higher accounts payable to merchants and increased Membership Rewards liabilities associated with growth in billed business.

nodes.title: Cash Flows from Investing Activities
nodes.summary:
## Cash Flows from Investing Activities

Our cash flows from investing activities primarily include changes in Card Member loans and receivables, as well as changes in our available-for-sale investment securities portfolio.

In 2022, the net cash used in investing activities was primarily driven by higher Card Member loan and receivable balances, resulting from higher Card Member spending and net purchases of investment securities.

In 2021, the net cash used in investing activities was primarily driven by higher Card Member loan and receivable balances, resulting from higher Card Member spending, partially offset by net maturities of our investment securities.

nodes.title: Cash Flows from Financing Activities
nodes.summary:
## Cash Flows from Financing Activities

Our cash flows from financing activities primarily include changes in customer deposits, long-term debt and short-term borrowings, as well as dividend payments and share repurchases.

In 2022, the net cash provided by financing activities was primarily driven by growth in customer deposits and net proceeds from debt, partially offset by share repurchases and dividend payments.

In 2021, the net cash used in financing activities was primarily driven by share repurchases, net debt repayments, decreases in customer deposits, dividends and redemption of preferred shares, partially offset by the proceeds from the issuance of preferred shares.

nodes.title: GOVERNANCE
nodes.summary: The partial document describes the governance structure and processes for risk management within the organization. It outlines the comprehensive Enterprise-wide Risk Management (ERM) program, led by the Chief Risk Officer, which is responsible for identifying, monitoring, and managing various types of risks. Oversight is provided by the Board of Directors through three independent committees: the Risk Committee (overseeing the ERM framework, risk appetite, and key risk exposures), the Audit and Compliance Committee (focusing on compliance, internal controls, and audit functions), and the Compensation and Benefits Committee (ensuring compensation practices align with prudent risk-taking). The document also details the roles of internal management committees, particularly the Enterprise Risk Management Committee (ERMC) and the Asset Liability Committee, in overseeing risk governance and financial risks. Additionally, it explains the "three lines of defense" model for risk management, delineating responsibilities among risk takers, independent risk oversight, and internal audit functions.

nodes.title: CREDIT RISK MANAGEMENT PROCESS
nodes.summary:
## CREDIT RISK MANAGEMENT PROCESS

We define credit risk as loss due to default or changes in the credit quality of a customer, obligor or security. Our credit risks are divided into two broad categories: individual and institutional. Each has distinct risk management capabilities, strategies, and tools. Business units that create individual or institutional credit risk exposures of significant importance are supported by dedicated risk management teams, each led by a Chief Credit Officer.

nodes.title: Individual Credit Risk
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses individual credit risk, focusing on consumer and small business credit products like charge cards, credit cards, and term loans. It highlights the diverse customer base and emphasizes the company's strong customer profile, attributed to brand reputation, customer service, product features, and robust risk management practices. The document outlines the roles of business unit leaders, Chief Credit Officers, and the Individual Credit Risk Committee (ICRC) in overseeing credit risk, ensuring policy compliance, and escalating issues as needed. It also describes the use of advanced proprietary scoring models and data-driven decision-making processes that leverage customer data and credit bureau information to manage credit risk and enhance customer interactions.

nodes.title: Institutional Credit Risk
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses institutional credit risk, highlighting that it primarily arises in the CS, ICS, and GMNS business units, as well as in investment and liquidity management activities. It notes that institutional credit risk differs from individual credit risk by having less frequent but potentially more severe losses, influenced by both economic conditions and client-specific events. The document outlines the governance structure for managing this risk, emphasizing the roles of Chief Credit Officers and the Institutional Risk Management Committee (IRMC). The IRMC is responsible for implementing credit risk policies, guiding credit officers, making investment decisions related to risk, ensuring adherence to underwriting standards, monitoring exposures, and determining risk mitigation actions. The IRMC also reviews large exposures for compliance and escalates issues as needed, while a centralized risk rating unit assesses institutional obligors. The overall aim is to optimize risk-adjusted returns on capital.

nodes.title: Exposure to the Airline and Travel Industry
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the company's significant exposure to the airline and travel industry through various cobrand, rewards, merchant acceptance, and corporate payment arrangements, particularly highlighting a major partnership with Delta. It outlines how the company's Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) program assesses risks associated with airline partners and the broader travel sector, including cruise lines, travel agencies, and tour operators. The document also references the competitive environment for partner relationships and the potential risks these partnerships pose, such as reputational issues, business disruptions, and financial obligations, directing readers to the "Risk Factors" section for more details.

nodes.title: Debt Exposure
nodes.summary:
## Debt Exposure

As part of our ongoing risk management process, we monitor our financial exposure to both sovereign and non-sovereign customers and counterparties, and measure and manage concentrations of risk by geographic regions, as well as by economic sectors and industries. A primary focus area for monitoring is credit deterioration due to weaknesses in economic and fiscal profiles. We evaluate countries based on the market assessment of the riskiness of their sovereign debt and our assessment of the economic and financial outlook and closely monitor those deemed high risk. As of December 31, 2022, we considered our gross credit exposures to government entities, financial institutions and corporations in those countries deemed high risk to be individually and collectively not material.

nodes.title: OPERATIONAL RISK MANAGEMENT PROCESS
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the organization's approach to operational risk management. It defines operational risk as losses resulting from inadequate or failed processes, people, systems, or external events, including regulatory non-compliance and third-party issues. The document describes a comprehensive operational risk framework governed by the Operational Risk Management Policy and overseen by the Operational Risk Management Committee (ORMC). Key elements of the framework include risk event capture, coordinated issue management, key risk indicators, and risk assessments at both process and entity levels. The framework emphasizes identifying, measuring, monitoring, and reporting operational risks, determining root causes, assessing impacts (operational, financial, brand, regulatory, legal), and assigning accountability for resolution and control enhancements.

nodes.title: Information and Cyber Security
nodes.summary: This partial document discusses American Express's approach to information and cyber security risk, defining it as the risk of incidents affecting the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of sensitive information. It outlines the company's comprehensive cyber security program, which is based on advanced technology, expert personnel, and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework. The program includes controls for identifying, protecting against, detecting, responding to, and recovering from security incidents. The document also notes ongoing investments in cyber security enhancements and participation in industry and government initiatives. It references additional details about the potential impacts of major security incidents under the "Risk Factors" section.

nodes.title: Information Technology
nodes.summary:
## Information Technology

We define information technology risk as the risk that events or circumstances could compromise the processing, stability, capacity, performance, or resilience of information technology and cause financial, reputational, and/or regulatory impacts.

We manage information technology risk through our policies, procedures, governance structure, and control framework to preserve the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of systems and processes across our Company.

See "The uninterrupted operation of our information systems is critical to our success and a significant disruption could have a material adverse effect on our business and results of operations" under "Risk Factors" for additional information.

nodes.title: Privacy
nodes.summary:
## Privacy

We define privacy risk as the risk of financial loss, reputational damage, or regulatory or legal action resulting from decisions related to the violation of applicable laws, rules, regulations, contractual obligations, or the non-adherence to privacy policies, disclosures, or standards that apply to the processing of personal data.

The Global Privacy Policy establishes the privacy framework and defines the American Express Data Protection \& Privacy Principles, which governs the way we collect, use, store, share, transmit, delete or otherwise process our customer and colleague personal data globally. Chaired by the Chief Privacy Officer, the Privacy Risk Management Committee, a sub-committee of the ORMC, provides oversight and governance for our privacy program.

nodes.title: Data Management and Governance
nodes.summary:
## Data Management and Governance

We define data management and governance risk as the risk of financial, reputational, and/or regulatory impacts due to inadequate data governance and/or data management practices adversely impacting the accuracy, completeness, timeliness, comprehensiveness or usability of data throughout its lifecycle.

Our Enterprise Data Governance Policy establishes the framework for defining in-scope critical data and the requirements for managing such data effectively throughout its lifecycle as a critical corporate asset. This policy is approved by the ERMC.

Chaired by the Chief Data Officer, our Enterprise Data Committee, a sub-committee of the ERMC, provides governance and oversight for our enterprise-wide data governance and management activities.

nodes.title: Third Party Risk
nodes.summary:
## Third Party Risk

We define third party risk as the risk that relationships with third parties (including their significant subcontractors) create unexpected outcomes and deviations from expectations or stated obligations. The Third Party Management Policy is approved by the Risk Committee of our Board and the ERMC. It sets forth the procurement, risk management, and contracting framework for managing third-party relationships commensurate with their risk and complexity. Our Third Party Lifecycle Management program sets guidelines for identifying, measuring, monitoring, and reporting the risk associated with third parties through the life cycle of the relationships, which includes planning, due diligence and third-party selection, contracting, ongoing monitoring and termination.

nodes.title: Conduct Risk
nodes.summary:
## Conduct Risk

We define conduct risk as the risk that colleagues, intentionally or unintentionally, fail to fulfill their responsibilities to American Express, our customers, colleagues or stakeholders in a manner consistent with our Code of Conduct, policies and values as well as applicable laws and regulations. Conduct issues also have the potential to increase several other risk types, including reputational risk, which may undermine the integrity and trust upon which our brand is built.

The Conduct Risk Management Policy is approved by the ERMC. It establishes the governance framework for conduct risk across the Company. The policy requires annual risk assessments, implementation of detective and preventive controls, colleague training and timely escalations of conduct issues. It also provides guidance on consequence management for any substantiated cases of misconduct. The Conduct Risk Committee oversees conduct risk related topics and escalates such matters to the ERMC, as appropriate.

nodes.title: COMPLIANCE RISK MANAGEMENT PROCESS
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the organization's approach to compliance risk management, defining compliance risk as the potential for legal, reputational, or financial harm due to non-compliance with laws, regulations, internal policies, or ethical standards. It describes the role of the Global Compliance and Ethics organization in establishing a company-wide Compliance Risk Management Program, which involves assessing, controlling, monitoring, measuring, and reporting compliance risks. The Compliance Risk Management Committee (CRMC), led by the Chief Compliance Officer, is tasked with identifying, evaluating, managing, and escalating compliance risks, and reports to both the ERMC and the Audit and Compliance Committee. The document also highlights the existence of a comprehensive Anti-Money Laundering program, including independent risk assessments and oversight by the Internal Audit Group to ensure adherence to regulatory guidance.

nodes.title: REPUTATIONAL RISK MANAGEMENT PROCESS
nodes.summary:
## REPUTATIONAL RISK MANAGEMENT PROCESS

We define reputational risk as the risk that negative stakeholder reaction to our products, services, client and partner relationships, business activities and policies, management and workplace culture, or our response to unexpected events, could cause sustained critical media coverage, a decline in revenue or investment, talent attrition, litigation, or government or regulatory scrutiny.

We view protecting our reputation for excellent customer service, trust, security and high integrity as core to our vision of providing the world's best customer experience and fundamental to our long-term success.

Our business leaders are responsible for considering the reputational risk implications of business activities and strategies and ensuring the relevant subject matter experts are engaged as needed. The ERMC is responsible for ensuring reputational risk considerations are included in the scope of appropriate subordinate risk policies and committees and properly reflected in all decisions escalated to the ERMC.

nodes.title: MARKET RISK MANAGEMENT PROCESS
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the organization's approach to market risk management. It defines market risk as the potential impact on earnings or asset and liability values from changes in market prices, specifically highlighting interest rate risk and foreign exchange risk. The document describes the governance structure, including the roles of the Market Risk Management Committee, the Market Risk Oversight Officer, and other committees such as the ERMC and Asset Liability Committee. It emphasizes the use of risk policies that set quantitative limits and escalation triggers, and notes that market risk management is also governed by policies related to derivatives, funding, liquidity, and investments, ensuring compliance with regulatory requirements.

nodes.title: Interest Rate Risk
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the company's approach to managing interest rate risk. It outlines how various interest rate scenarios are analyzed to assess potential impacts on earnings, asset and liability values, and the economic value of equity. The document explains the use of interest rate swaps to manage exposure between fixed and variable-rate debt. It provides a specific sensitivity analysis, stating that a hypothetical 100 basis point increase in market interest rates would negatively affect annual net interest income by approximately $141 million. The analysis includes assumptions about the repricing behavior of assets and liabilities, particularly deposits, based on historical experience. The document also notes that actual impacts may differ due to various influencing factors.

nodes.title: Foreign Exchange Risk
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the company's exposure to foreign exchange risk, identifying four main sources: card member spending in foreign currencies, cross-currency funding activities, cross-currency investing (such as foreign subsidiaries), and revenues/expenses in foreign currencies. It explains that these risks are managed primarily through foreign exchange spot and forward contracts, with $34 billion in notional amounts outstanding as of December 31, 2022. The document provides sensitivity analysis, stating that a hypothetical 10% strengthening of the U.S. dollar would have an immaterial impact on earnings and equity from most exposures, but could reduce pretax income by approximately $153 million for anticipated foreign currency earnings over the next year. It also notes that market risk from the Foreign Exchange International Payments business is minimized through hedging and limits, and that the actual impact of rate changes depends on various factors including timing, hedging activities, and business mix.

nodes.title: FUNDING \& LIQUIDITY RISK MANAGEMENT PROCESS
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the company's approach to funding and liquidity risk management. It defines funding and liquidity risk as the inability to meet financial and business obligations at a reasonable cost. The document describes the governance structure, including a Board-approved Liquidity Risk Policy and oversight by the Funding and Liquidity Committee. The company aims to maintain diverse and accessible liquidity sources to cover business needs and financing obligations for at least twelve months, even during adverse economic conditions. The management process involves balancing the costs and risks of holding liquidity, monitoring liquidity at both the consolidated and subsidiary levels, reviewing cash forecasts, approving funding plans for normal and stressed scenarios, setting liquidity guidelines, and taking necessary actions based on ongoing monitoring.

nodes.title: MODEL RISK MANAGEMENT PROCESS
nodes.summary:
## MODEL RISK MANAGEMENT PROCESS

We define model risk as the risk of adverse consequences, such as financial loss, poor business and strategic decision making, damage to our reputation or customer harm, from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs and outcomes.

The Enterprise-Wide Model Risk Policy establishes the comprehensive framework for governing model risk. This policy is approved by the ERMC. The comprehensive risk management and governance framework includes procedures for model development, independent model validation, model risk reporting and change management capabilities that seek to minimize erroneous model methodology, outputs, and misuse. We also assess model performance and modelrelated issues on an ongoing basis and seek to address deficiencies in a timely manner. In addition, we utilize artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) models for a variety of business use cases. We perform extensive reviews and testing to reduce the risk that these AI/ML techniques result in adverse consequences.

nodes.title: STRATEGIC AND BUSINESS RISK MANAGEMENT PROCESS
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the company's approach to strategic and business risk management. It defines strategic and business risk as the potential failure to achieve business objectives due to poor strategic decisions, inadequate implementation, or declining demand. The document describes a structured process where strategic decisions are reviewed and approved by business leaders and committees to ensure alignment with company policies. Risk controls are integrated into decision-making processes, and ongoing oversight is provided over business goals. Product performance is periodically reviewed, and significant actions such as mergers, acquisitions, and divestitures require thorough due diligence, comprehensive risk assessments, and approval from senior risk officers or committees. Additionally, all new or materially changed products and services undergo review and approval by specialized committees to manage associated risks.

nodes.title: COUNTRY RISK MANAGEMENT PROCESS
nodes.summary:
## COUNTRY RISK MANAGEMENT PROCESS

We define country risk as the risk that economic, social, and/or political conditions and events in a country present. They might adversely impact us, primarily as a result of greater credit losses, increased operational or market risk or the inability to repatriate capital.

We manage country risk as part of the normal course of business. Policies and procedures establish country risk escalation thresholds to control and limit exposure, driven by processes that enable the monitoring of conditions in countries where we have exposure.

nodes.title: ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL AND GOVERNANCE (ESG) AND CLIMATE-RELATED RISK
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the organization's approach to Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) and climate-related risks. It defines climate-related risk as encompassing both transition risks (arising from the shift to a low-carbon economy, including policy, legal, technological, market, and reputational risks) and physical risks (stemming from acute events like extreme weather and chronic changes such as sea level rise). The document highlights that climate-related risks can impact various aspects of the business, including customers, operations, and suppliers, and can manifest as different types of financial and operational risks. The organization is enhancing its risk governance framework to better address climate-related risks, treating them as an emerging risk and undertaking processes to identify, measure, and manage these risks.

title: CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES
summary:
The partial document discusses the company’s critical accounting estimates, focusing on areas that require significant management judgment and assumptions. The main points covered include:

1. **Reserves for Card Member Credit Losses**: The document explains the methodology for estimating expected credit losses on card member loans and receivables, primarily using the CECL (Current Expected Credit Loss) model. It details the use of quantitative and qualitative components, the role of macroeconomic scenarios, and the significant judgments involved, such as determining the reasonable and supportable period (R&S Period), modeling default probabilities, and incorporating economic forecasts. The sensitivity of credit loss estimates to changes in macroeconomic assumptions is also discussed.

2. **Membership Rewards Liability**: The estimation process for the liability associated with the company’s Membership Rewards program is described. This includes the use of statistical and actuarial models to estimate the ultimate redemption rate (URR) and the weighted average cost (WAC) per point. The document highlights the factors affecting these estimates, such as redemption trends, card member behavior, and changes in partner contracts, and notes the high degree of judgment involved.

3. **Goodwill Recoverability**: The process for testing goodwill for impairment is outlined, including both qualitative and quantitative assessments. The quantitative assessment involves estimating the fair value of reporting units using income (discounted cash flows) and market approaches, with significant judgment required in forecasting cash flows, selecting discount rates, and choosing market comparables.

4. **Income Taxes**: The document covers the complexities of accounting for income taxes, including the establishment of provisions for income tax expense, the recognition and measurement of unrecognized tax benefits, and the realization of deferred tax assets. It emphasizes the judgment required in interpreting tax laws, assessing the sustainability of tax positions, and estimating the likelihood of realizing deferred tax assets.

Overall, the document highlights the areas of financial reporting that involve substantial management judgment and estimation uncertainty, and discusses the potential impact of changes in assumptions or economic conditions on the company’s financial statements.

title: OTHER MATTERS
summary:
The partial document covers several key areas:

1. Disclosure of an internal review regarding uncredited Membership Rewards points for certain U.S. Card Members with multiple cards, noting the issue was resolved with an immaterial financial impact in 2022.
2. Reference to recently issued and adopted accounting standards, directing readers to another section for details.
3. A comprehensive glossary defining important financial and operational terms used by the company, including metrics and concepts related to card products (e.g., Card Member loans, receivables, cards-in-force), revenue streams (e.g., discount revenue, processed revenue), spending categories (e.g., T&E-related volume, G&S-related volume), financial ratios (e.g., capital ratios, net write-off rates), and other industry-specific terminology (e.g., asset securitizations, loyalty coalitions, cobrand cards).
4. Explanations of non-GAAP financial measures and how certain metrics are calculated, providing context for understanding the company’s financial statements and performance indicators.

title: CAUTIONARY NOTE REGARDING FORWARD-LOOKING STATEMENTS
summary: The partial document is a "Cautionary Note Regarding Forward-Looking Statements" from a financial report, warning readers that statements about future expectations, plans, and performance are subject to significant risks and uncertainties. It outlines numerous factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from those projected, including: macroeconomic conditions (such as inflation, interest rates, recession risks, and labor market issues); geopolitical instability (notably the Russia-Ukraine conflict); impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic; regulatory and legal developments; competitive pressures in the payments industry; changes in consumer and business spending; credit performance and risk management; marketing and operating expenses; tax rates; capital and liquidity management; technology and cybersecurity risks; international expansion challenges; ESG initiatives; and the financial health of business partners. The document emphasizes that these risks could affect revenue growth, profitability, customer behavior, product innovation, and the company’s ability to execute strategic initiatives, and it refers readers to additional risk disclosures elsewhere in the company’s filings.

title: MANAGEMENT'S REPORT ON INTERNAL CONTROL OVER FINANCIAL REPORTING
summary: This partial document is Management’s Report on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting. It outlines management’s responsibility for establishing and maintaining adequate internal controls to ensure the reliability of financial reporting and compliance with U.S. GAAP. The report describes the objectives of internal controls, including accurate record-keeping, proper authorization of transactions, and prevention or timely detection of unauthorized asset use. It acknowledges inherent limitations of internal controls and the potential for their effectiveness to change over time. Management assessed the effectiveness of internal controls as of December 31, 2022, using the COSO Internal Control — Integrated Framework (2013), and concluded that controls were effective as of that date. The report also notes that PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP has provided an independent audit report on the effectiveness of these controls.

nodes.title: Basis for Opinions
nodes.summary: This partial document outlines the responsibilities of both the company's management and the external auditors regarding the consolidated financial statements and internal control over financial reporting. It explains that management is responsible for preparing the financial statements and maintaining effective internal controls, while the auditors are responsible for expressing opinions on these matters. The document details the auditing standards followed (PCAOB standards), the requirement for auditor independence, and the procedures performed during the audit, including risk assessment, testing of evidence, evaluation of accounting principles and estimates, and assessment of internal controls. The auditors conclude that their procedures provide a reasonable basis for their opinions.

nodes.title: Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: This partial document defines internal control over financial reporting as a process intended to ensure the reliability of financial reporting and the proper preparation of financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP). It outlines the key components of such controls, including maintaining accurate records, ensuring transactions are properly authorized and recorded, and safeguarding assets against unauthorized use or disposition. The document also discusses the inherent limitations of internal controls, noting that they may not always prevent or detect misstatements and that their effectiveness can be affected by changes in conditions or compliance over time.

nodes.title: Reserves for Credit Losses on Card Member Loans
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the process and considerations involved in estimating and auditing reserves for credit losses on Card Member loans. It explains that management determines these reserves based on expected lifetime credit losses, using statistical models that incorporate historical loss experience, current and future economic conditions, and significant management judgment. Key areas of judgment include the selection of the reasonable and supportable period (R&S Period), modeling of probability and exposure at default, and the use of qualitative reserves to address model limitations or external factors. The document also highlights that auditing these reserves is considered a critical audit matter due to the complexity and subjectivity involved, requiring specialized skills to evaluate management’s methodology, significant inputs, assumptions, and the effectiveness of related controls.

nodes.title: Membership Rewards Liability
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the Membership Rewards liability as reported in the consolidated financial statements, specifically focusing on how management estimates the cost of Membership Rewards points expected to be redeemed in the future. It details the key assumptions used in this estimate, including the Ultimate Redemption Rate (URR) and the Weighted Average Cost (WAC) per point, and explains the statistical and actuarial models applied to determine these assumptions. The document highlights the significant judgment and complexity involved in estimating the URR, which makes auditing this liability a critical audit matter. It outlines the audit procedures performed, such as testing controls, verifying the completeness and accuracy of model inputs, involving specialists to independently estimate the URR, and comparing the auditor’s calculations to management’s estimates. The section concludes with the auditor’s signature and a statement of their tenure as the company’s auditor. Additionally, an index to the consolidated financial statements and related notes is provided, listing the contents and page numbers of the financial statement sections and accompanying notes.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF INCOME
nodes.summary: The partial document presents the Consolidated Statements of Income for the years ended December 31, 2022, 2021, and 2020. It details the company’s revenues, breaking them down into non-interest revenues (such as discount revenue, net card fees, service fees, and processed revenue) and interest income (from loans, investment securities, and deposits). The statement also outlines interest expenses, net interest income, and total revenues net of interest expense. Provisions for credit losses are reported, followed by total revenues after these provisions. The document then lists major expense categories, including card member rewards, business development, card member services, marketing, salaries and benefits, and other expenses, leading to pretax income, income tax provision, and net income. Earnings per common share (basic and diluted) and average common shares outstanding are also provided, along with explanatory notes regarding the calculation of earnings per share.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF COMPREHENSIVE INCOME
nodes.summary: The partial document presents the Consolidated Statements of Comprehensive Income for the years 2022, 2021, and 2020. It details net income figures for each year, followed by components of other comprehensive income, including net unrealized gains or losses on debt securities, foreign currency translation adjustments, and pension and postretirement benefit adjustments, all net of tax. The document then summarizes total other comprehensive income (or loss) and provides the comprehensive income for each year, showing how these items impact overall financial performance.

- Cash flow activities are categorized into operating, investing, and financing activities, with net cash provided by operating activities increasing in 2022, significant cash outflows from investing activities, and substantial inflows from financing activities.

- The document provides a snapshot of the company’s financial position and liquidity, highlighting changes in key financial metrics over the reported periods.

The main points covered include the impact of accounting changes (specifically the adoption of the CECL methodology), net income, other comprehensive losses, repurchases of common shares, issuance and redemption of preferred shares, changes related to employee plans, and the declaration of cash dividends for both preferred and common shares. The table provides year-end balances for each component of shareholders' equity and highlights significant transactions affecting equity during each year.

title: SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
summary:
This partial document outlines the Summary of Significant Accounting Policies for a global payments company. The main points covered include:

1. **Company Overview**: The company provides credit and charge card products, as well as travel and lifestyle services, to a diverse global customer base through multiple channels.

2. **Principles of Consolidation**: The financial statements are prepared in accordance with US GAAP, with details on how entities are consolidated based on controlling financial interest, including voting interest entities and variable interest entities (VIEs). Equity method and fair value accounting for investments are also described.

3. **Foreign Currency**: Policies for translating and remeasuring foreign currency transactions and subsidiaries are explained, including the treatment of translation adjustments.

4. **Use of Estimates and Assumptions**: Management’s use of estimates in preparing financial statements is discussed, highlighting key areas such as credit losses, rewards liabilities, goodwill, and income taxes.

5. **Revenue Recognition**: The document details when and how revenue is recognized for various streams, including discount revenue from merchants, net card fees, service fees, processed revenue, and contra-revenue arrangements.

6. **Interest Income and Expense**: Methods for recognizing interest income from loans, investments, and deposits, as well as interest expense related to funding and debt, are described.

7. **Card Member Rewards and Business Development**: Accounting for rewards programs, business development expenses, and payments to partners is outlined.

8. **Card Member Services and Marketing**: Recognition of expenses related to value-added services and marketing activities is explained.

9. **Balance Sheet Items**: Policies for cash and cash equivalents, goodwill (including impairment testing), premises and equipment (including depreciation and software capitalization), and leases (including right-of-use assets and lease liabilities) are provided.

10. **Other Significant Accounting Policies**: A table references additional policies such as loans and receivables, credit loss reserves, investment securities, securitizations, legal contingencies, derivatives, fair value measurements, guarantees, and income taxes, with cross-references to relevant notes.

11. **Classification and Reclassification**: Notes that certain prior period amounts may be reclassified for consistency.

12. **Recently Issued and Adopted Accounting Standards**: Summarizes recent changes in accounting standards, including updates on troubled debt restructuring and the adoption of the CECL methodology for credit losses, and their impact on the company’s financial statements.

title: LOANS AND CARD MEMBER RECEIVABLES
prefix_summary:
# LOANS AND CARD MEMBER RECEIVABLES

Our lending and charge payment card products that we offer to consumer, small business and corporate customers result in the generation of Card Member loans and Card Member receivables. We also extend credit to customers through non-card financing products, resulting in Other loans.

nodes.title: CARD MEMBER AND OTHER LOANS
nodes.summary: This partial document section discusses the accounting and presentation of Card Member and Other Loans. It explains that Card Member loans are recorded when a cardholder makes a purchase, include revolve-eligible transactions, finance charges, and fees, and are subject to minimum payments and finance charges if balances are revolved. The terms of these loans can vary and be updated. Card Member loans are shown on the balance sheet net of reserves for credit losses, and interest accrual stops when accounts are written off. Other loans refer to non-card consumer and commercial credit products, which have fixed terms and are governed by separate agreements. These are also presented net of reserves for credit losses. The section provides a table showing the balances of Card Member and Other loans as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, including breakdowns by consumer, small business, and corporate segments, as well as details on reserves for credit losses and the inclusion of certain loans related to consolidated variable interest entities (VIEs) and Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loans.

nodes.title: CARD MEMBER RECEIVABLES
nodes.summary: This partial document discusses Card Member receivables, explaining that these are amounts due from cardholders for transactions and fees, which must be paid in full by the payment due date. It distinguishes between different types of cardholders (Consumer, Small Business, Corporate) and presents the receivable balances for each as of December 31, 2022 and 2021. The document also details the reserves for credit losses deducted from gross receivables to arrive at net receivables, and notes that a portion of corporate receivables is associated with a consolidated variable interest entity (VIE).

nodes.title: CARD MEMBER LOANS AND RECEIVABLES AGING
nodes.summary: This partial document section discusses the aging of Card Member loans and receivables, defining accounts as past due if payment is not received within 30 days after the billing statement date. It presents detailed tables showing the breakdown of outstanding balances for consumer, small business, and corporate accounts as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, categorized by how many days payments are past due (current, 30-59, 60-89, and 90+ days). The document also explains that for corporate accounts, delinquency is tracked differently (by days past billing), and that data for periods other than 90+ days past billing is not available for these accounts due to system constraints. The information is intended to provide insight into the credit quality and risk management of the card member portfolio.

nodes.title: CREDIT QUALITY INDICATORS FOR CARD MEMBER LOANS AND RECEIVABLES
nodes.summary: This partial document presents key credit quality indicators for card member loans and receivables as of and for the years ended December 31, 2022 and 2021. It includes tables showing net write-off rates (both principal only and including interest/fees) and the percentage of accounts 30+ days past due, broken down by consumer, small business, and corporate segments. The document explains the methodology for calculating write-off rates, notes system constraints for certain corporate data, and highlights a significant recovery related to a corporate client bankruptcy in 2021. It also references additional qualitative factors considered in credit loss reserves, as detailed in another note.

nodes.title: IMPAIRED LOANS AND RECEIVABLES
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the company's approach to impaired loans and receivables, defining them as loans for which it is probable that not all contractual amounts will be collected. It outlines the criteria for classifying loans as impaired, including loans over 90 days past due, non-accrual loans, and those modified as troubled debt restructurings (TDRs). The document explains the modification programs offered to customers experiencing financial difficulty, such as temporary interest rate reductions, fixed payment plans, and suspension of delinquency fees, and details how accounts are classified as "In Program" or "Out of Program" TDRs. It describes the measurement of reserves for TDRs using discounted cash flow models and includes tables presenting data on impaired loans and receivables by category (consumer, small business, corporate, other loans) for the years 2020, 2021, and 2022, including total impaired balances and reserves for credit losses. The footnotes clarify specific terms and data classifications used in the tables.

nodes.title: LOANS AND RECEIVABLES MODIFIED AS TDRs
nodes.summary: The partial document provides detailed information on loans and receivables that were modified as Troubled Debt Restructurings (TDRs) over the years 2020, 2021, and 2022. It presents tables showing the number of accounts, account balances, average interest rate reductions, and average payment term extensions for different categories, including Card Member Loans, Card Member Receivables, and Other Loans. The document also includes footnotes explaining the calculation of balances, the nature of modifications, and the types of loans involved. Additionally, it provides data on the number and balances of TDR-modified accounts that subsequently defaulted within twelve months of modification, broken down by year and loan type. The information highlights trends in TDR activity, the impact of modifications, and subsequent default rates.

title: RESERVES FOR CREDIT LOSSES
summary:
The partial document discusses the methodology and key considerations for establishing reserves for credit losses on Card Member loans and receivables. It explains the use of the CECL (Current Expected Credit Loss) model, which incorporates historical loss experience, current and forecasted economic conditions, and various statistical models (Probability of Default, Exposure at Default, and Recovery models) to estimate expected credit losses over a reasonable and supportable period. The document details how macroeconomic scenarios, such as unemployment rates and GDP growth, are factored into reserve calculations, and how management applies judgment to adjust reserves for qualitative factors not captured by quantitative models. It also outlines the process for writing off uncollectible loans and receivables.

Additionally, the document provides tables and analysis of changes in reserves for credit losses on Card Member loans and receivables for the years ended December 31, 2022, 2021, and 2020. It highlights the drivers behind increases or decreases in reserves, such as changes in loan and receivable balances, delinquency rates, macroeconomic forecasts, and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. The tables present beginning and ending reserve balances, provisions, net write-offs, and other adjustments for each year.

title: INVESTMENT SECURITIES
summary:
The partial document provides a detailed overview of the company’s investment securities as of December 31, 2022 and 2021. It covers the following main points:

- Investment securities primarily consist of available-for-sale debt securities and equity securities, both carried at fair value on the Consolidated Balance Sheets.
- The methodology for estimating credit losses on available-for-sale debt securities is described, including the assessment of credit indicators, recognition of credit losses through income statements, and treatment of unrealized gains and non-credit losses in comprehensive income.
- Accrued interest on available-for-sale debt securities is reported as other assets.
- Equity securities are also carried at fair value, with unrealized gains and losses recognized in income.
- Realized gains and losses from securities sales are recognized using the specific identification method.
- A summary table presents the cost, gross unrealized gains and losses, and estimated fair value of various categories of investment securities for 2022 and 2021, including state and municipal obligations, U.S. government and agency obligations, mortgage-backed securities, foreign government bonds, other debt securities, and equity securities.
- Additional tables break down available-for-sale debt securities in unrealized loss positions by the length of time in loss and by the ratio of fair value to amortized cost.
- The document explains that most unrealized losses are due to increases in benchmark interest rates, not credit deterioration, and management does not expect to sell the securities at a loss or experience credit losses.
- Weighted average yields and contractual maturities for available-for-sale debt securities are provided, with notes on the potential for early calls or prepayments and the calculation of yields on a tax-equivalent basis.

title: ASSET SECURITIZATIONS
summary: The partial document discusses American Express's asset securitization activities, specifically the periodic securitization of Card Member loans and receivables through the transfer of these assets to two securitization trusts: the American Express Credit Account Master Trust (Lending Trust) and the American Express Issuance Trust II (Charge Trust). These trusts issue debt securities collateralized by the transferred assets to third-party investors. The trusts are classified as variable interest entities (VIEs), and American Express is identified as the primary beneficiary due to its servicing role, decision-making authority, and significant ownership of variable interests in the trusts. The document details the amounts of variable interests held, the non-recourse nature of the issued debt securities, the restricted cash balances within the trusts, and the conditions under which triggering events could affect the trusts' operations. It also notes that no such triggering events occurred during the years ended December 31, 2022 and 2021.

title: OTHER ASSETS
summary: The partial document provides a detailed summary of "Other Assets" as of December 31, 2022 and 2021. It includes a breakdown of goodwill, other intangible assets (at amortized cost), and other assets (such as net deferred tax assets, receivables, investments in non-consolidated entities, prepaid assets, tax credit investments, and right-of-use lease assets). The document discusses changes in goodwill by operating segment, including acquisitions, dispositions, and foreign currency translation effects, and notes that a quantitative goodwill impairment assessment was performed with no impairment recognized. It also covers other intangible assets, their amortization schedules, accumulated amortization, and expected future amortization expenses. Additionally, the document explains the accounting for tax credit investments, particularly qualified affordable housing (QAH) investments, including their carrying amounts, unfunded commitments, off-balance sheet obligations, and the recognition of investment losses and associated tax credits.

title: CUSTOMER DEPOSITS
summary: The partial document provides a detailed breakdown of customer deposits as of December 31 for the years 2022 and 2021. It categorizes deposits by region (U.S. and Non-U.S.) and by type (interest-bearing and non-interest-bearing), including specific mention of Card Member credit balances. The document further classifies deposits by deposit type, such as savings and transaction accounts, certificates of deposit (direct and brokered), sweep accounts, other deposits, and Card Member credit balances. It also presents the scheduled maturities of certificates of deposit by year, and discloses the aggregate amount of certificates of deposit in denominations of $250,000 or more, separated by U.S. and Non-U.S. holdings.

title: DEBT
summary: The partial document provides a detailed overview of the company's debt as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, covering both short-term and long-term borrowings. It includes tables summarizing outstanding balances, interest rates, and maturities for various types of debt, such as senior notes, subordinated notes, and borrowings from different company entities. The document also describes the company's access to committed credit facilities and secured borrowing facilities, their usage, associated fees, and key terms such as the absence of material adverse change clauses and credit rating dependencies. Additionally, it outlines aggregate annual maturities of long-term debt, compliance with financial covenants, and total interest paid over recent years.

title: OTHER LIABILITIES
summary: This partial document provides a detailed summary of "Other Liabilities" as of December 31 for two consecutive years, breaking down the main components such as Membership Rewards liability, deferred card and other fees (net), employee-related liabilities, card member rebate and reward accruals, income tax liability, and other miscellaneous liabilities. It explains the nature of each liability, including specific notes on employee benefits, tax obligations (notably the repatriation tax under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act), and various accruals and payables. The document also describes the Membership Rewards program, outlining how the liability is estimated using actuarial models and key assumptions like the weighted average cost per point and ultimate redemption rate. Additionally, it details the calculation of deferred card and other fees, net of acquisition costs and reserves for cancellations, and provides a table reconciling these amounts for both years.

title: STOCK-BASED COMPENSATION
summary:
The partial document provides a detailed overview of the company’s stock-based compensation programs. It covers the following main points:

- Description of the company’s Incentive Compensation Plans, including the types of awards granted (stock options, restricted stock units (RSUs), and other incentives), eligibility, and the number of shares available for grant as of year-end 2022, 2021, and 2020.
- Summary of stock-based compensation expense recognized in the financial statements for 2022, 2021, and 2020, along with related income tax benefits.
- Tabular summary of stock option and RSU activity during 2022, including grants, exercises/vestings, forfeitures, and outstanding balances, with weighted-average prices.
- Explanation of the accounting for stock-based compensation expense, including recognition over the vesting period and retirement eligibility considerations.
- Details on stock options: grant terms, vesting schedules, contractual life, fair value estimation using the Black-Scholes-Merton model, and key assumptions used for 2022, 2021, and 2020. Special mention of performance- and market-based option grants to certain executives and their valuation using a Monte Carlo model.
- Information on the remaining contractual life, aggregate intrinsic value, and unrecognized compensation cost for outstanding and exercisable stock options as of December 31, 2022.
- Data on stock option exercises, including intrinsic value realized, cash received, and related income tax benefits for 2022, 2021, and 2020.
- Description of RSUs, including service-based and performance-based awards, vesting schedules, performance metrics (including a relative total shareholder return modifier), and dividend entitlements.
- Valuation methods for RSUs, including use of grant-date stock price and Monte Carlo modeling for performance-based RSUs, with key assumptions disclosed.
- Disclosure of unrecognized compensation cost and vesting periods for RSUs, as well as the fair value of RSUs granted and vested in recent years.
- Overview of liability-based awards that may be settled in cash or equity, their classification as liabilities, remeasurement process, and cash paid upon vesting in 2022, 2021, and 2020.

title: RETIREMENT PLANS
summary: The partial document discusses the company’s retirement plans, focusing on two main types: defined contribution retirement plans and defined benefit pension and other postretirement benefit plans. It describes the primary defined contribution plan, the Retirement Savings Plan (RSP), a 401(k) with profit-sharing, and provides annual global expense figures for these plans from 2020 to 2022. For defined benefit pension and other postretirement benefit plans, it notes that the main plans in the US and UK are closed to new entrants and no longer accrue benefits, while some employees in other countries have local plans or receive retirement payments as required by law. The document also mentions unfunded postretirement plans offering health care and life insurance to certain retired US employees, with net benefit figures for recent years. It explains how the funded status of these plans is recognized on the balance sheet, providing the unfunded status amounts as of the end of 2022 and 2021.

title: CONTINGENCIES AND COMMITMENTS
summary:
The partial document discusses the company's contingencies and commitments. Under "Contingencies," it outlines various ongoing and potential legal proceedings involving the company and its subsidiaries, including class actions and regulatory investigations related to antitrust, consumer protection, tax, and contractual matters. Specific cases are described, such as lawsuits regarding anti-steering provisions, liability shifts for credit card transactions, and antitrust tying arrangements. The document details the status and potential financial impact of these proceedings, including accruals for probable losses and an estimated range of possible additional losses up to $200 million beyond current accruals. It also notes ongoing regulatory reviews and tax disputes in multiple jurisdictions.

Under "Commitments," the document provides information on lease expenses and liabilities, including the total lease expense for recent years, the present value of outstanding lease commitments, and the schedule of future lease payments. It also discloses approximately $2.0 billion in financial commitments to cobrand partners, which are tied to minimum payment agreements over several years, primarily based on card member activity.

title: DERIVATIVES AND HEDGING ACTIVITIES
summary:
The partial document discusses the company’s use of derivative financial instruments as part of its risk management strategy to manage exposures to market risks, specifically interest rate and foreign exchange risks. It explains that derivatives are not used for trading purposes but to hedge risks arising from the company’s operations, such as funding activities and foreign currency transactions. The document details how interest rate risk is managed through a mix of variable- and fixed-rate funding and the use of interest rate swaps, while foreign exchange risk is managed through spot agreements and derivatives like foreign exchange forwards.

The document also addresses counterparty credit risk associated with derivatives, describing the use of master netting agreements, collateral requirements, and credit support agreements to mitigate this risk. It notes that most derivative positions are subject to netting and collateralization, and that the company monitors the creditworthiness of counterparties.

A table summarizes the fair value of derivative assets and liabilities as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, distinguishing between derivatives designated as hedging instruments (fair value hedges and net investment hedges) and those not designated as hedges. The document explains the accounting treatment for derivatives, including hedge effectiveness assessments and the impact of derivatives on the company’s financial statements.

Specific types of hedges are described:
- Fair value hedges: Used to hedge exposure to changes in the fair value of fixed-rate debt, with interest rate swaps converting fixed rates to floating rates. The effectiveness and financial impact of these hedges are quantified.
- Net investment hedges: Used to hedge currency exposure of investments in foreign subsidiaries, with gains and losses recorded in accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI).
- Derivatives not designated as hedges: Used for economic hedging of foreign currency transactions, with gains and losses recognized in income.

The document also mentions an embedded derivative related to an equity method investee, its fair value, and the resulting gains recognized in income. Overall, the partial document provides a comprehensive overview of the company’s derivatives and hedging activities, risk management practices, accounting treatment, and the financial impact of these instruments.

title: FAIR VALUES
summary:
The partial document provides a comprehensive overview of the company’s approach to fair value measurement and disclosure for financial assets and liabilities, in accordance with GAAP. The main points covered include:

1. **Definition of Fair Value and Hierarchy**: The document defines fair value and explains the three-level GAAP fair value hierarchy (Levels 1, 2, and 3), detailing the types of inputs used at each level and the frequency of monitoring and evaluation.

2. **Recurring Fair Value Measurements**: It presents tables summarizing the company’s financial assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a recurring basis as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, categorized by the fair value hierarchy. The assets include investment securities (equity and debt), derivatives, and the associated levels. Liabilities primarily include derivatives.

3. **Valuation Techniques for Recurring Measurements**: The document describes the valuation methods used for investment securities and derivatives, including the use of quoted prices, pricing services, discounted cash flow models, and Monte Carlo simulations for complex Level 3 instruments. It also discusses the process for validating and corroborating prices from third-party sources.

4. **Fair Value of Financial Instruments Not Carried at Fair Value**: Tables summarize the estimated fair values of financial assets and liabilities measured at amortized cost (not at fair value), such as cash, loans, certificates of deposit, and long-term debt, with breakdowns by hierarchy level and explanations of the estimation techniques used.

5. **Valuation Techniques for Non-Recurring Measurements**: The document outlines the methods for estimating fair value for assets and liabilities not carried at fair value, including discounted cash flow models for loans and CDs, and market-based approaches for long-term debt.

6. **Nonrecurring Fair Value Measurements**: It discusses assets measured at fair value on a nonrecurring basis, such as equity investments without readily determinable fair values, the process for recognizing impairments, and the use of Level 3 measurements when impairment indicators are present. It also provides data on unrealized gains and losses for these investments.

7. **Disclosure References**: The document references additional notes for more detailed information on specific asset and liability categories.

Overall, the partial document details the company’s policies, methodologies, and disclosures related to fair value measurement, including both recurring and nonrecurring fair value assessments, and provides quantitative and qualitative information on the valuation of its financial instruments.

title: GUARANTEES

# GUARANTEES

The maximum potential undiscounted future payments and related liability resulting from guarantees and indemnifications provided by us in the ordinary course of business were $\$ 1$ billion and $\$ 21$ million, respectively, as of December 31, 2022 and $\$ 1$ billion and $\$ 24$ million, respectively, as of December 31, 2021, all of which were primarily related to our real estate arrangements and business dispositions.

To date, we have not experienced any significant losses related to guarantees or indemnifications. Our recognition of these instruments is at fair value. In addition, we establish reserves when a loss is probable and the amount can be reasonably estimated.

It includes a table summarizing the number of authorized, issued, and outstanding common shares for the years 2020-2022, as well as details on share repurchases, stock option exercises, and shares reserved for employee plans. The document also notes the full redemption of Series B and C preferred shares in 2021 and confirms that no warrants were outstanding as of the end of 2022, 2021, and 2020.

title: CHANGES IN ACCUMULATED OTHER COMPREHENSIVE INCOME (LOSS)
summary: The partial document discusses the changes in Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI), a component of shareholders' equity on the balance sheet, over the three years ended December 31, 2022. It details the balances and annual changes in AOCI's main components: net unrealized gains (losses) on debt securities, foreign currency translation adjustments (net of hedges), and net unrealized pension and other postretirement benefit gains (losses). The document provides a table showing the year-end balances and changes for each component, as well as a separate table outlining the related tax impacts for each year. It also notes that reclassifications out of AOCI into the income statement were not significant during the period.

nodes.title: Section 1. Effective Date

## Section 1. Effective Date

The original effective date of this Deferred Compensation Plan for Directors and Advisors (this "Plan") was October 1, 1973. This Plan was most recently amended and restated on April 1, 2018. This Plan is further amended and restated as provided herein effective January 1, 2023.

nodes.title: Section 2. Eligibility
nodes.summary:
## Section 2. Eligibility

Any Director of or Advisor to the Board of Directors of American Express Company (the "Company") and/or any Director of American Express National Bank ("AENB," successor by conversion and merger to American Express Centurion Bank and American Express Bank, FSB) (hereinafter a "Director" or an "Advisor") who is not an officer or employee of the Company, AENB or a subsidiary thereof is eligible to participate in this Plan. All deferral and related elections in effect under this Plan prior to the date hereof on behalf of any Director of or Advisor to the Company and any Director of AENB, American Express Centurion Bank and American Express Bank, FSB eligible to participate in this Plan shall continue to apply until such elections are revoked or revised.

nodes.title: Section 3. Administration
nodes.summary:
## Section 3. Administration

The Nominating and Governance Committee (the "Committee") of the Board of Directors shall administer this Plan. The Committee shall have all the powers necessary to administer this Plan, including the right to interpret the provisions of this Plan and to establish rules and prescribe any forms for the administration of this Plan. The Committee may delegate its authority under this Plan to the Company's Corporate Secretary (the "Administrator") to take administrative and other specified actions, subject to such terms and limitations as the Committee may impose.

nodes.title: Section 4. Deferral Elections
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the rules and procedures for Directors to elect to defer receipt of either 50% or 100% of their compensation for service as a Director or Advisor, including committee service. It specifies the timing requirements for making a deferral election, generally requiring elections to be made before the start of the year in which compensation is earned, with special provisions for newly elected Directors to make an irrevocable election within 30 days of joining the Board. The document also addresses the effective dates of such elections depending on when they are received by the Administrator, and states that, unless changed or revoked, a deferral election will continue to apply to subsequent years. All provisions are subject to compliance with Section 409A of the Internal Revenue Code.
